titleText.es: Vi por primera vez este problema en el test de aptitud de Google Labs. Un profesor y yo llenamos una pizarra sin conseguir nada. Divertíos.
titleText.en: I first saw this problem on the Google Labs aptitude test. A professor and I filled a blackboard without getting anywhere. Have fun.
titleText.noteEn: The archive title literally means “Nerd Hunting,” while the official English title is “Nerd Sniping.” The Spanish title text closely translates the official source; divertíos is an informal plural command used mainly in Spain.

regions.labelEs: HAY UN CIERTO TIPO DE CEREBRO QUE SE INCAPACITA CON FACILIDAD.
SI LE ENSEÑAS UN PROBLEMA INTERESANTE, LO ABANDONA TODO INVOLUNTARIAMENTE PARA PONERSE A ELLO.

applications.explanationEn: Si introduces a genuinely possible condition, and enseñas uses the ordinary present form for one familiar listener; le identifies the receiver between them.
Le points back to the previously named type of brain as the receiver of what is shown.
The printed lo attempts to carry the original English “it” as the doer, but standard Spanish would leave that already understood doer unstated before abandona.
Para introduces the purpose, and poner remains in its unchanged dictionary form inside ponerse.
Se attaches directly to the unchanged verb poner and makes the printed result one word.
Ponerse keeps the action in its dictionary form with se attached, a supplies the fixed link, and ello points back to the task already mentioned.

regions.labelEs: ESTO ME HA LLEVADO A INVENTAR UN NUEVO DEPORTE: LA CAZA DE NERDS. ¿VES A ESE FÍSICO CRUZANDO?

applications.explanationEn: Ha is the present helper for one subject, and llevado is llevar's completed-action form.
Me identifies the affected speaker, ha llevado gives the completed prompting action, a supplies the required link, and inventar stays in its dictionary form.
A marks the specific person receiving the seeing action, and ese físico identifies that person.
Ves addresses one familiar observer, a ese físico identifies the person seen, and cruzando presents that person's action as in progress.
Oye is the irregular positive command of oír used to get one familiar listener's attention.

regions.labelEs: En esta malla infinita de resistencias ideales de 1 omh, ¿cuál es la resistencia equivalente entre los dos nodos señalados?

excludedUnits.rationale: This is the printed numerical resistance measurement, including the source's misspelling omh for ohm, not Spanish lexical vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Cuál keeps its written accent because it directly asks for the unknown value.

regions.labelEs: ES... MMM. INTERESANTE. QUIZÁ SI EMPEZAMOS POR... NO. ESPERA. MMM, PODRÍAMOS...

applications.explanationEn: Si introduces the tentative possible condition, and empezamos uses the ordinary present form for “we.”
Empezamos supplies the form for “we,” and por would introduce the first step, which the trailing interruption leaves unstated.
Espera is the regular positive command directed to one familiar listener.
Poder keeps its complete dictionary form and adds -íamos for a tentative possibility involving “we.”

excludedUnits.rationale: This elongated impact and vehicle sound effect is not Spanish lexical vocabulary.

regions.labelEs: NO TENGO NADA QUE VER CON ESTO.

applications.explanationEn: Ver contributes the fixed expression's idea of connection or relevance here rather than its ordinary literal sense “to see.”

applications.exampleEs: NO TENGO NADA QUE VER CON ESTO
applications.explanationEn: Tengo changes for the speaker, nada que ver forms the fixed core about having no connection, and con esto supplies the matter from which the speaker distances himself.

regions.labelEs: VENGA, HAZTE UN CARTEL. ¡ES DIVERTIDO! LOS FÍSICOS SON DOS PUNTOS, LOS MATEMÁTICOS, TRES.

applications.explanationEn: Venga stands alone here as an encouraging conversational “come on,” rather than as a literal request for someone to come.
Haz is the irregular positive command of hacer for one familiar listener, with te attached.
Te is written on the end of the positive command haz and presents the result as made or obtained for the listener.
Tres supplies the second score; the earlier son and puntos remain understood instead of being printed again.

applications.exampleEs: LOS FÍSICOS SON DOS PUNTOS, LOS MATEMÁTICOS, TRES
applications.explanationEn: The first part supplies the full scoring pattern. After the comma, los matemáticos changes the group and tres changes the value, while son and puntos are left understood.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; presents the thing as changing
cards.noteEn: With verbs such as reducir and ampliar, se lets Spanish describe a change without naming anyone who causes it. English often uses a simple verb such as “shrinks” or “widens.”

cards.answerEn: becomes disabled; becomes unable to function (with se)
cards.noteEn: Incapacita is a present form of incapacitar. With se before it, the person or thing being described enters a disabled or nonfunctioning state rather than disabling something else.

example.es: El sistema se incapacita con el calor.
example.en: The system becomes unable to function in the heat.

cards.noteEn: Facilidad names ease or lack of difficulty. Con facilidad describes how something happens and is naturally translated as “easily.”

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce a real or possible condition with “if”?
cards.answerEn: Use si without an accent, followed by an ordinary present-time verb form.
cards.noteEn: This pattern treats the condition as genuinely possible. Spanish normally does not put a future-tense verb directly after si in this kind of condition; the result can appear separately as a statement, prediction, or command.

cards.answerEn: may have no separate English word; marks the thing receiving the effect
cards.noteEn: Le can appear before a verb even when a later phrase beginning with a names the receiver explicitly. English normally states that receiver only once.

example.es: Le cambié la rueda al coche.

cards.answerEn: you show (one familiar person or thing)
cards.noteEn: Enseñas is the present form of enseñar used for tú, one familiar listener. Enseñar can mean either “to teach” or “to show”; the surrounding object decides which sense applies.

cards.answerEn: “it” here, but this is nonstandard Spanish; standard Spanish would omit lo
cards.noteEn: Lo normally stands for the person or thing receiving an action; it does not name who or what performs that action. Spanish usually leaves an already understood performer unstated because the verb form carries it. A standard version would say abandona todo without lo.

example.es: La máquina falla y abandona la tarea.
example.en: The machine fails and abandons the task.

cards.noteEn: Abandona is a present form used with one person or thing. With todo, it describes dropping or leaving everything else aside.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.answerEn: to get started; to get to work (on something)
cards.noteEn: Ponerse is the dictionary form poner with se attached. In ponerse a ello, it describes turning one's attention to a matter and beginning work on it.

example.es: Tenemos tiempo para ponernos a trabajar.
example.en: We have time to get to work.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone gets started on a matter or task already mentioned?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of ponerse, then a ello.
cards.noteEn: Ponerse changes for the person and time: me pongo, te pones, se pone, nos ponemos, and so on. Ello points back to the matter or task, while a is the required link between the two parts.

example.es: Después de comer, nos ponemos a ello.
example.en: After lunch, we get to work on it.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links ponerse to ello
cards.noteEn: Ponerse a ello requires a between ponerse and ello. Translating this a by itself as “to” would sound unnatural in English.

example.en: Now I will get to work on it.

cards.noteEn: Ello is a small neutral reference word that can point back to an idea, event, or task rather than to a masculine or feminine object. It is more common in formal writing and in fixed expressions such as ponerse a ello.

example.en: We will talk about it tomorrow.

cards.noteEn: Esto is a neutral demonstrative for an unidentified thing, fact, or whole situation. It is not used directly before a noun.

cards.promptEs: llevar a alguien a + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that something leads or prompts someone to do an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of llevar, mark the affected person, then add a and the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Llevar changes for the person and time doing the leading. The affected person can appear as me, te, lo, la, nos, los, las, or a named person. The final action stays in its unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir.

example.es: La curiosidad me llevó a preguntar.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: Llevado is the completed-action form of llevar. After ha and before a plus another verb, it says that something has led or prompted someone to do an action.

example.es: La duda me ha llevado a preguntar.
example.en: The doubt has led me to ask.

cards.answerEn: to (linking a verb to the following infinitive)

cards.noteEn: Caza can name the activity of hunting or a hunt itself.
Nerd is an English loanword also used informally in Spanish for a highly intellectual or technically absorbed person. This printed plural keeps the English -s.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that you see someone while that person is doing an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of ver, then a before the person, followed by the action form ending in -ando or -iendo.
cards.noteEn: Ver changes for who sees. A marks the person being seen, and the final -ando or -iendo form presents that person's action as in progress: correr becomes corriendo and caminar becomes caminando.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a specific person as the object
cards.noteEn: Spanish generally places a before a specific person who receives a verb’s action. This “personal a” is not translated as a separate English word.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.
Ese points to a masculine singular noun that is not presented as right next to the speaker. Feminine singular is esa.

example.en: I do not recognize that sound.

cards.noteEn: Físico can be an adjective meaning “physical,” but here it is a noun for a person who works in physics.
Cruzando is the ongoing-action form of cruzar. Regular -ar verbs replace -ar with -ando for this form.

example.es: Veo a Pablo cruzando la plaza.
example.en: I see Pablo crossing the square.

cards.noteEn: Oye is the informal singular command form of oír, “to hear.” In conversation it commonly gets one person's attention, like “hey” or “listen.”

example.en: Hey, I need to talk to you.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.
In an electrical diagram, malla describes a gridlike network of connected branches rather than a piece of fabric.

example.es: La corriente pasa por una malla de resistencias.
example.en: The current passes through a grid of resistors.

cards.noteEn: Infinita has a feminine ending because it describes the feminine noun malla.
In a circuit, resistencia can name either opposition to electric current or a component—a resistor—that provides it. The diagram makes the component sense prominent here.

example.en: We connect two resistors to the circuit.

cards.noteEn: In a technical problem, ideal describes components treated as perfectly matching a simplified model, without real-world imperfections.

cards.answerEn: what; which one (asking for an identity or value)
cards.noteEn: Before es or son, cuál often asks the listener to identify the answer or value. Natural English frequently uses “what” even though cuál is related to “which.”

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

cards.noteEn: Electrical resistance measures how strongly a component or network opposes electric current.

cards.answerEn: the single resistance that would have the same electrical behavior between two terminals as the whole network
cards.noteEn: A network of many resistors can sometimes be represented, from two chosen connection points, by one resistance that produces the same relationship between voltage and current. Finding that value simplifies the network without claiming that its internal layout is the same.

example.es: Calculamos la resistencia equivalente entre A y B.
example.en: We calculate the equivalent resistance between A and B.

cards.answerEn: nodes; connection points in a network
cards.noteEn: In a circuit diagram, a node is a point where connected wires or components share the same electrical potential.

example.es: Los cables se unen en dos nodos.
example.en: The wires join at two nodes.

cards.noteEn: Señalados describes the masculine plural nodos and points to the ones marked in the diagram.

cards.answerEn: hmm; a sound of hesitation or thought
cards.noteEn: Mmm represents a pause while someone thinks, hesitates, or considers an idea.
Empezamos is the present form of empezar used for nosotros or nosotras, “we.”

example.en: We start with the first question.

cards.promptEs: empezar/comenzar por + primera cosa o acción
cards.questionEn: How do you identify the first item or action in a sequence?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of empezar or comenzar, then por, then the first thing or action.
cards.noteEn: The verb changes for the person and time. After por, use a noun or an unchanged action verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. This pattern means ‘start with’ or ‘start by.’

example.en: We will start by reviewing the data.

cards.noteEn: After empezar or comenzar, por can introduce the first thing or action in an ordered process.

cards.answerEn: we could (a possibility or tentative suggestion)
cards.noteEn: Podríamos is the “would/could” form of poder for “we.” Poder keeps its whole dictionary form and adds -íamos. It often makes a suggestion sound tentative rather than stating a firm plan.

cards.questionEn: How do you form a Spanish “would” verb such as “would forget”?
cards.answerEn: Keep the whole dictionary form and add a conditional ending such as -ía.
cards.noteEn: The same endings attach to verbs ending in -ar, -er, and -ir. The ending changes for the person: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, or -ían.

cards.promptEs: no tener nada que ver con…
cards.answerEn: Use no tener nada que ver con…: “to have nothing to do with…”
cards.noteEn: This is a fixed expression; ver does not mean literally “to see” here. Use con to name the unrelated subject. You can leave that subject unsaid when the conversation already makes it clear.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that one thing has no connection to another?

example.es: Eso no tiene nada que ver con el precio.
example.en: That has nothing to do with the price.

cards.noteEn: After a negative verb, nada is commonly translated as “anything,” even though its basic meaning is “nothing.” Spanish keeps both negative words.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word (part of nada que ver)
connection; relevance (inside nada que ver con)
cards.noteEn: Ver normally means “to see.” Inside no tener nada que ver con, however, it is part of a fixed expression about having no connection or involvement; translating ver alone as “see” would be misleading.

example.es: Eso no tiene nada que ver con el precio.
example.en: That has nothing to do with the price.

cards.noteEn: Haz is the irregular positive command of hacer for one familiar listener. Te is attached to its end and presents the result as being made or obtained for that listener.

example.en: Make yourself a cup of tea.

cards.promptEs: imperativo afirmativo de tú + pronombre al final
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the command and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: A positive command tells someone to do something, rather than not to do it. With one informal listener, sienta + te becomes siéntate. A written accent may be added so the combined word keeps the original stress. In a negative command, the short word goes before the verb instead: no te sientes.
cards.questionEn: If a positive command includes a short word such as te (“yourself”) or lo (“it”), where does that word go?

cards.promptEs: primera afirmación; segunda persona, cosa o valor con palabras repetidas omitidas
cards.questionEn: Can Spanish leave out repeated words in the second part of a comparison or list?
cards.answerEn: Yes. State the full first part, then keep only the changed person, thing, or value when the repeated words are already clear.
cards.noteEn: This omission is called ellipsis: words are understood even though they are not repeated. A comma or semicolon often marks the gap. The listener recovers the missing verb and other repeated material from the first parallel part.

example.es: Ana tiene dos libros; Luis, tres.
example.en: Ana has two books; Luis has three.

cards.noteEn: As a noun, físicos names people who work in physics. The same written form can be an adjective meaning “physical” when it describes a plural masculine noun.

cards.answerEn: points in a score or numerical scale
cards.noteEn: Punto can mean a dot, a location, or a point in a score or measured scale. The plural puntos counts units on that scale, whether they are awarded in a game or used to state a measured score.
